exam-04-q01.why_correct_en: The Battle of Waterloo is the correct answer. It was fought on 18 June 1815 near Waterloo in present-day Belgium, then part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. Wellington's multinational allied army and Blücher's Prussians defeated Napoleon, who abdicated again and was exiled to St Helena. The question calls it the last battle between Britain and France; more precisely, it was the decisive final battle of the Napoleonic Wars and Britain fought as part of a coalition.

exam-04-q02.why_correct_en: The daffodil is associated with Wales and is commonly worn, together with the leek, on St David's Day on 1 March. Its national status is more recent than the leek's. A useful language link is that leek is cennin in Welsh, while daffodil is cennin Pedr; daffodils also flower around St David's Day.

exam-04-q03.why_correct_en: The destruction was caused by the Great Fire of London in 1666, during Charles II's reign. It began on 2 September at Thomas Farriner's bakery in Pudding Lane and spread rapidly through a dry, densely packed, timber-built city. About 13,200 houses, 87 parish churches and the old St Paul's Cathedral were destroyed. The rebuilt cathedral was designed by Christopher Wren.

exam-04-q04.why_correct_en: Every five years is the maximum interval implied by the life of a Parliament, not a promise that every election will be exactly five years after the previous one. Parliament may be dissolved earlier. At dissolution every Commons seat becomes vacant and MPs seeking to return must stand again; polling normally follows a 25-working-day timetable.

exam-04-q05.why_correct_en: True. Authorised Scottish banks issue genuine pound sterling notes that can be used elsewhere in the UK. However, Scottish notes are not legal tender in either England or Scotland, and legal tender has only a narrow meaning concerning settlement of debts. A business may choose which payment methods to accept, so 'valid everywhere' does not mean every shop must take them.

exam-04-q06.why_correct_en: The National Trust is the conservation charity that protects historic buildings, gardens, archaeology, countryside and coastline. Founded in 1895, it now looks after roughly a quarter of a million hectares of land and 890 miles of coastline across England, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland has a separate organisation, the National Trust for Scotland.

exam-04-q07.why_correct_en: True. Great Britain comprises England, Scotland and Wales and does not include Northern Ireland. The United Kingdom is Great Britain together with Northern Ireland. The British Isles is a wider geographical term that also includes Ireland, the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, which are not all parts of the UK.

exam-04-q08.why_correct_en: Boudicca, queen of the Iceni, led a major revolt against Roman rule in AD 60–61. Roman seizure of her late husband's kingdom and violence against Boudicca and her daughters were important causes. The rebels destroyed Colchester, London and St Albans before Roman troops defeated them. Boudicca later became a powerful symbol of resistance.

exam-04-q09.why_correct_en: Winston Churchill placed first in the BBC's 2002 Great Britons public poll. The main historical memory point is his wartime leadership: he became Prime Minister in May 1940, insisted that Britain continue fighting Nazi Germany, led a cross-party government, rallied the public through speeches and worked with Franklin D. Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin in the Allied coalition.

exam-04-q10.why_correct_en: The two Houses are the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Both make laws, scrutinise government and debate public issues, and most Bills need approval from both before Royal Assent. The Commons is elected and has primacy over taxation and government confidence; the Lords revises legislation and provides further scrutiny.

exam-04-q11.why_correct_en: In 1928 the Equal Franchise Act lowered women's voting age to 21 and removed the different property restrictions, giving women the vote on the same basis as men. About five million additional women became eligible. The 1918 reform had enfranchised only women aged 30 or over who met specified qualifications.

exam-04-q12.why_correct_en: The monarch is the exam answer, but the precise title is Supreme Governor of the Church of England. The monarch does not manage everyday church teaching or worship. The Archbishops of Canterbury and York lead the Church's direction, with Canterbury as its most senior bishop. This role applies only to the Church of England, not every church in the UK.

exam-04-q13.why_correct_en: The Grand National is a long-distance horse-racing steeplechase held at Aintree near Liverpool. Its early form began in 1839 as the Grand Liverpool Steeplechase. Red Rum is the memorable champion: it won in 1973, 1974 and 1977 and remains the only horse to have won the Grand National three times.

exam-04-q14.why_correct_en: Poems is the exam answer. Geoffrey Chaucer's late-14th-century Canterbury Tales uses a pilgrimage to Canterbury as a frame in which travellers from different social groups tell stories. Most of the work is Middle English verse, although a few tales are in prose. Its literary importance includes demonstrating that English could carry major literature when French and Latin remained prestigious.

exam-04-q15.why_correct_en: Christmas Day is 25 December and commemorates the birth of Jesus Christ. It is a UK bank holiday. When 25 December falls at a weekend, a substitute weekday may be observed as the bank holiday, but Christmas Day itself remains 25 December. Boxing Day is the following day, 26 December.

exam-04-q16.why_correct_en: The Cavaliers were the Royalists who supported Charles I in the Civil Wars beginning in 1642; Parliament's supporters were called Roundheads. The conflicts concerned royal authority, Parliament's rights over taxation and government, and religion. Parliament's New Model Army prevailed, Charles I was executed in 1649, and the monarchy was restored in 1660.

exam-04-q17.why_correct_en: The Bayeux Tapestry depicts the events around the 1066 Norman Conquest, including the Battle of Hastings. Despite its name, it is an embroidery made with coloured wool on linen, roughly 70 metres long, and was probably made in England. It also preserves details of 11th-century ships, weapons, clothing and food.

exam-04-q18.why_correct_en: Anne Boleyn was executed inside the Tower of London. Henry VIII's second wife and Elizabeth I's mother was convicted after a trial Historic Royal Palaces describes as a sham. On 19 May 1536 she was beheaded by a French swordsman on Tower Green and buried in the Chapel Royal of St Peter ad Vincula.

exam-04-q19.why_correct_en: Criminal offences are prohibited by public law and may be investigated by police or another enforcement authority and prosecuted in a criminal court. Racially aggravated offending can attract more serious treatment, while smoking in prohibited enclosed public places can result in a fixed penalty or prosecution. These differ from private civil disputes such as contracts or compensation claims.

exam-04-q20.why_correct_en: A tramp is the correct answer: Charlie Chaplin's Little Tramp wore a bowler hat, toothbrush moustache and cane with a tight coat, baggy trousers and oversized shoes. Chaplin designed the costume as a set of contradictions. The poor character borrowed a gentleman's symbols and often outwitted authority, making the comedy understandable worldwide without spoken dialogue.

exam-04-q21.why_correct_en: False. A candidate for the UK House of Commons must be at least 18, not 21, and must have an eligible British, Irish or Commonwealth citizenship status and not be legally disqualified. Party membership is not required: independent candidates may stand. Formal nomination also normally requires specified paperwork and a £500 deposit.

exam-04-q22.why_correct_en: Sir Robert Watson-Watt led the development of Britain's practical aircraft-detection radar rather than inventing every form of radar alone. A 1935 demonstration showed that reflected radio waves could locate aircraft. His work led to the Chain Home coastal early-warning network, which fed information into RAF Fighter Command during the Battle of Britain.

exam-04-q23.why_correct_en: 10 Downing Street is both the Prime Minister's official residence and working office. In 1735 George II offered the property to Robert Walpole, who asked that it be assigned to future First Lords of the Treasury rather than given to him personally. The building is much larger than its façade suggests, and the door's letterbox still bears that formal title.

exam-04-q24.why_correct_en: Television and Radio are the exam answers because broadcasters are subject to statutory due-impartiality rules under the Communications Act 2003 and Ofcom's Broadcasting Code. The phrase 'equal time' is an oversimplification: due impartiality does not require identical airtime for every view. During elections broadcasters give parties, candidates and significant perspectives due weight; newspapers and ordinary online publishers are not governed by the same broadcast rules.
